title: Help my unbelief (Mark 9:14–29)
hookLine: a desperate father: I believe; help my unbelief
last: LET IT CHANGE WHAT YOU DO.

lines: IF THOU CANST DO ANY THING.
cards: From the shining mountain straight down into a mess: a crowd, and an argument. The disciples who stayed behind have tried to heal a boy, and they couldn't. The boy's father pushes through.
His son, he says, has a spirit that takes his speech, throws him to the ground, makes him foam and grind his teeth and go rigid. Since he was a child. It has thrown him into fire and into water.
Years of nights like that, and now even the disciples have failed. His hope is worn thin. In the King James Bible he says: "if thou canst do any thing, have compassion on us, and help us."

teach.b: Jesus catches the word and hands the if back. In the King James text: "If thou canst believe, all things are possible to him that believeth."
And the father cries out, with tears: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Both at once. I believe, and I don't.
I trust you, and I'm terrified. He doesn't pretend. And Jesus doesn't send him away to come back when his faith is tidier.
He heals the boy, and lifts him by the hand. In Mark's telling, half a faith, handed over honestly, is where it starts. The Greek word for unbelief is apistia, faith with a no in front of it.
Some Christians call this verse a lifeline, because it puts doubt and faith in the same sentence. Readers today often notice that the boy's signs sound like epilepsy.
Mark describes a spirit, and Christians understand stories like this in different ways. Later, the disciples ask privately why they failed.
His answer, in the King James: "This kind can come forth by nothing, but by prayer and fasting."

teach.h: A WEEK OF SEEING IN PART.
teach.b: Now look back at the week. Seven baskets: enough again. Hard hearts in a boat: do you not yet understand?
A blind man seeing men like trees.

teach.h: LORD, I BELIEVE; HELP THOU MINE UNBELIEF.
teach.b: Peter: you are the Christ. Take up your cross. Listen to him.
And now this father. Again and again this week, someone sees in part, and is helped further along.

how: Some Christians pray the father's words, "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief," as a short prayer in times of doubt, and some pastors point to this story to say that faith and doubt can live together.

o: unbelief: faith with a no in front of it
a sickness that throws a person down
a strong faith that never once doubts

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.
p: if thou canst do any thing

s: Jesus told the father to come back when his faith was stronger
he healed the boy on the spot, half a faith and all.
the father said I believe and help my unbelief in one breath
"Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief."
the disciples asked their question in front of the crowd
they asked him privately, in the house: why could not we cast him out?

games.q: you're the father. you've tried everything, and his friends have failed. now you're face to face with Jesus. what do you say?
games.why: he says both: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." and Jesus doesn't wait for a tidier faith. the boy is healed.

practice: Think of one thing you trust and one thing you doubt, about God, about yourself, about someone you love, and let them sit side by side without solving either.

If you pray, you can say the father's words, slowly, as many times as you like: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. If you don't pray, you can simply say: some of me trusts, some of me doesn't, and that's where I am.

wordCard.voice: Apistia, faith with a no in front of it: a father's cry holding belief and doubt in the same breath, and it was enough.

orig.note: Greek: unbelief. pistis, faith, with a- in front: not.

carryVoice: Your line: bring the half you have. Half sure is enough to bring. Another week, done.
